strengths: The submission tackles an important yet rarely-trodden inverse imaging problem.

The submission is very open with its limitations which is an absolute breath of fresh air in modern papers. For example, L078 gives a much needed disclaimer about the risk of hallucinations from generative models in ill-posed medical image reconstruction problems. The submission’s discussion does a great job of listing limitations as well.
Overall, the submission is very clearly and straightforwardly presented and was a very easy read.
The proposed method use half or less measurement to achieve the same performance with the compared methods.
The paper contains a really good explanation of the novel approach.
The approaches, results and limitations of already existing work is well discussed.
Reducing the dose or measurement time during the CT measurement is an essential problem.
Novel combination of diffusion models with active learning.
The results are well discussed and compared to different baselines.
The paper tackles an important problem in the field of limited-angle CT. Long-scan times and high radiation doses clearly pose hurdles in all applications from medical tests to chip analysis.
The solution is well-motivated. By identifying the angles with the most uncertainty, the proposed method promises to select the next angle with the most information.
The experiments demonstrate notable gains in PSNR using the active learning approach versus the uniform sampling.
weaknesses: The same method was presented in Elata, et al ECCV 2024; the reviewer asks the authors to enumerate the technical differences between the works so readers can have clear takeaways.
The acquisition function is different between the two papers, but their covariance-based acquisition function appears to be benchmarked inadvertently in the Appendix and they perform identically.
Missing Active CT baselines: the reviewer asks why prior active learning for CT reconstruction works were not discussed or benchmarked, and suggests adding such comparisons if feasible.
Only CT experiments: the reviewer questions why other sensor-domain reconstruction problems such as MRI were not studied, and whether MRI active learning methods could be adapted for CT baselines.

No low-dose / sparse-view baselines: the reviewer requests discussion of differences between the proposed method and existing low-dose reconstruction methods, and whether regularizers such as TV can be used in the proposed setup.

Only simulated data: the reviewer notes that the paper uses only simulated synthetic X-ray projection data, which may cause an "inverse crime" and asks for justification for not using real measured projection datasets.

Technical contribution: the paper is viewed as a combination of Hard Data Consistency (Song et al 2023) and uncertainty sampling, but the proposed "soft" data consistency (hard DC + early stopping) is not ablated; the reviewer asks for an ablation study.
Runtime requirements are not reported; the reviewer wants quantification of the additional computational overhead associated with the method.
Minor typo: L462: "on pair" should be corrected to "on par".
Comparison with active learning method is preferred, such as the method proposed in [1]; please compare reconstruction result and inference time using the same number of projection angles.
The experiment is performed with parallel radon transform; more complex settings, such as fan-beam or 3D cone beam, should be used to verify the effectiveness of the proposed method.

The inference time is a huge disadvantage because n round k times sampling and n times full view projection are required; the reviewer asks for discussion of potential ways to mitigate the computational cost and a detailed analysis of the trade‑off between computational cost and reconstruction quality.

The improvement of the result may come from the diffusion model; the reviewer requests comparison with DPS or the proposed method without the active loop using uniform projection angles (27, 15, 18 angles) to isolate the benefit of the active learning component.

Pre‑training of the diffusion model is necessary; the computational cost of training such models can be substantial, potentially limiting practical applicability especially when datasets are small or frequently changing, and introduces a bottleneck in the workflow.

The diffusion model is highly dependent on the trained data; this raises concerns about generalizability to datasets that differ significantly from the training data, and performance could degrade considerably.
The diffusion model could introduce undesirable biases; the reviewer stresses the need for careful evaluation and mitigation of such biases as they could lead to systematic errors in reconstruction.
How to get the posterior distribution could be discussed in more detail; the method for obtaining the posterior distribution, crucial for the active learning strategy, is not sufficiently elaborated.

The contributions of the paper are not explicitly clear; it is unclear whether the main contribution is the diffusion model for sampling, the active learning procedure, or their combination, and the reviewer suggests stating contributions as bullet points in the introduction.

The structure of the experimental section is confusing, particularly Section 4.2; there is no context for methods such as SWAG and Bootstrap, and it is unclear where they are utilized in the framework; the reviewer suggests renaming the subsection to "Comparison Methods".
The paragraph from lines 468–473 lacks context; it is unclear which Table/Figure the analysis is discussing.

The practical advantage of active sampling with the diffusion approach is not convincing; since diffusion models are computationally heavy and slow, the reviewer wants evidence that the reduction in measurements offset the longer collection time per measurement.
In Line 300‑301, it would be useful to use a different variable rather than t to avoid confusion with the diffusion time steps.
